extracted.intended_audience: readers (and writers) of 18th‑century essays / general literate public
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and use of Samuel Johnson's Idler essays (mid‑18th century moral and social essays) for insight into human character, satire, and persuasive moral argument. Useful to readers and creative writers studying characterization, voice, and social observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect reciprocal scrutiny when using ridicule or censure
rubrics_metrics.description: It commonly happens to him who endeavours to obtain distinction by ridicule or censure, that he teaches others to practise his own arts against himself; and that, after a short enjoyment of the applause paid to his sagacity, or of the mirth excited by his wit, he is doomed to suffer the same severities of scrutiny, to hear inquiry detecting his faults, and exaggeration sporting with his failings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a practical axiom for satirists and critics: if you set yourself up to judge or deride others publicly you should expect and be prepared for similar examination and attack. Avoid assuming an unasked-for position of moral or critical authority ('seat[ing] himself uncalled in the chair of judicature'). This is both a rhetorical caution (anticipate counterattack) and an ethical one (critique invites reciprocity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Depict motives behind social pleasure (show superficial vs genuine pleasures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is therefore seldom such as it appears to others, nor often such as we represent it to ourselves. Of the ladies that sparkle at a musical performance, a very small number has any quick sensibility of harmonious sounds. But every one that goes has her pleasure. She has the pleasure of wearing fine clothes... she has the pleasure of appearing among other ladies... she has the pleasure of escaping for two hours the superiority of a sister, or the control of a husband...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When portraying characters in settings of public amusement, do not assume expressed aesthetic delight is the true motive. Show layered, often social or status‑based motives (vanity, display, avoidance of domestic power). Use specific incidental pleasures to reveal characters' real incentives rather than relying on generic statements of 'they enjoyed it.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use particular, repeated foibles/obsessions to reveal character
rubrics_metrics.description: Every man may be observed to have a certain strain of lamentation, some peculiar theme of complaint, on which he dwells in his moments of dejection. Jack's topick of sorrow is the want of time... For the omission of any civilities, want of time is his plea to others; for the neglect of any affairs, want of time is his excuse to himself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give characters a characteristic obsession or habitual excuse (e.g., 'want of time') and show how it contradicts their behaviour (Jack wastes time). Repetition of a small trait makes satire and characterization effective and believable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contrast rival narratives to expose bias (present multiple perspectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: For this reason every historian discovers his country; and it is impossible to read the different accounts of any great event, without a wish that truth had more power over partiality... Let us now oppose to this English narrative the relation which will be produced, about the same time, by the writer of the age of Louis XV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To illuminate partiality and rhetorical shaping, present competing accounts of the same event rather than a single authoritative narrative. Use contrasted diction, emphasis, and selective facts to demonstrate how perspective and national/biasing interests alter representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground thought and interior life in observable causes
rubrics_metrics.description: It is reasonable to believe, that thought, like every thing else, has its causes and effects; that it must proceed from something known, done, or suffered; and must produce some action or event... To every act a subject is required. He that thinks must think upon something.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rendering interiority, give characters concrete antecedents (past events, sensations, desires) that prompt reflection. Avoid presenting thought as an undifferentiated stream without referent; link mental states to experience and consequences to make inner life credible and narratively useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray friendship and relationships as contingent and changeable
rubrics_metrics.description: The friendship which is to be practised or expected by common mortals, must take its rise from mutual pleasure, and must end when the power ceases of delighting each other... Friendship is often destroyed by opposition of interest... The most fatal disease of friendship is gradual decay, or dislike hourly increased by causes too slender for complaint...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid idealized permanence in depicting friendships. Show how absence, shifting interests, small slights, and minute ambitions erode relationships. Use gradual, cumulative causes as realistic drivers of estrangement rather than single melodramatic events alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use examples and small scenes to argue social/political points
rubrics_metrics.description: The confinement, therefore, of any man in the sloth and darkness of a prison, is a loss to the nation, and no gain to the creditor... The end of all civil regulations is to secure private happiness from private malignity; but this end is apparently neglected, when a man, irritated with loss, is allowed to be the judge of his own cause...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making moral or political arguments in an essay, illustrate principles with concrete social examples and show systemic implications (e.g., imprisonment of debtors harms society). Use rhetorical exposition supported by particulars to persuade rather than relying on abstract assertion alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal universal human folly by aggregating commonplace behaviours
rubrics_metrics.description: All assemblies of gaiety are brought together by motives of the same kind... To every place of entertainment we go with expectation and desire of being pleased; we meet others who are brought by the same motives; no one will be the first to own the disappointment; one face reflects the smile of another, till each believes the rest delighted, and endeavours to catch and transmit the circulating rapture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To critique or illuminate human nature, depict how ordinary reciprocal behaviors create collective illusions (e.g., simulated delight). Use cumulative, small interactions (mirroring smiles, social contagion) to show how social fictions are maintained and how they deceive both actors and observers.
